steps.body: A **scatter plot** shows **paired data** — two numbers measured on each thing. Each dot uses one measurement for its across-position (x) and the other for its up-position (y). One dot per item.

widget.prompt: A plant is 3 weeks old and 5 cm tall. Plot the point (weeks = 3, height = 5).

pointErrors.feedback: You swapped the numbers — weeks (3) is the across-value and height (5) is the up-value: plot (3, 5).
The height is 5, not 3 — go up to 5: plot (3, 5).
The plant is 3 weeks old, so go across to 3: plot (3, 5).

widget.missFeedback: Each dot pairs the two measurements — across for weeks, up for height.
widget.successFeedback: Plotted — across to 3 weeks, up to 5 cm.

predict.prompt: The plant is 3 weeks old and 5 cm tall. Would plotting (5, 3) land on the same spot as (3, 5)?
predict.reveal: Order carries meaning: the first number is always the across, the second the up. Swap them and the plant teleports.

cml.actionGoal: Place ordered pairs and coordinate each observation across two quantitative variables.

steps.body: The two measurements must stay in order: the first number is always the across-value, the second the up-value. Swapping them puts the dot in the wrong place and can hide the real pattern in the data.

explanationVariants: A dot at across-4, up-7 represents the pair (4, 7): 4 hours studied, 7 problems solved.
Read across first (4), then up (7): the pair is (4, 7).

widget.prompt: On a study-time scatter plot (x = hours, y = problems solved), a dot sits at across-position 4, up-position 7. What pair does it show?

options.label: 4 hours, 7 problems
options.feedback: Right — across is hours (4), up is problems (7).

options.label: 7 hours, 4 problems
options.feedback: That swaps them — across (4) is hours, up (7) is problems: 4 hours, 7 problems.

options.label: 11 total
options.feedback: A scatter point shows a PAIR, not a sum — it's 4 hours and 7 problems.

options.label: 4 problems, 7 hours
options.feedback: The across-axis is hours (4) and the up-axis is problems (7): 4 hours, 7 problems.

widget.prompt: A student studied 2 hours and solved 4 problems. Plot the point (hours = 2, problems = 4).

pointErrors.feedback: You swapped them — hours (2) is across, problems (4) is up: plot (2, 4).
The student solved 4 problems, so go up to 4: plot (2, 4).
The problems value is 4, not 6 — plot (2, 4).

widget.missFeedback: Across for hours, up for problems.
widget.successFeedback: Plotted — across to 2 hours, up to 4 problems.

explanationVariants: Each item (each student) contributes exactly one dot, holding its two measurements.
One dot represents one item's pair of values.

widget.prompt: On a scatter plot of 10 students' height and shoe size, how many dots appear?

options.label: 10 — one dot per student
options.feedback: Right — each student is one dot holding both measurements.

options.label: 20 — two per student
options.feedback: Each student is ONE dot; the two measurements are its across and up positions, not two dots.

options.label: 2 — one per measurement
options.feedback: The plot has one dot per STUDENT (10), not one per measurement.
It's one dot per student: 10 dots.

explanationVariants: A scatter plot reveals how two quantities move together — a relationship a single-variable plot can't show.
Pairing lets you see whether one measurement relates to the other.

widget.prompt: What can a scatter plot show that a plot of just one measurement cannot?

options.label: Whether the two measurements are related
options.feedback: Right — pairing the data reveals a relationship between the two quantities.

options.label: The exact average of one measurement
options.feedback: A single-variable plot shows an average fine — the scatter plot's job is the RELATIONSHIP between two.

options.label: Nothing new
options.feedback: It shows something new: how the two measurements move together.

options.label: Only the largest value
options.feedback: It reveals the relationship between two measurements, not just an extreme value.

explanationVariants: A 5-week-old, 6-cm plant is the pair (5, 6): across to 5, up to 6.
Across for weeks (5), up for height (6): plot (5, 6).

widget.prompt: A second plant is 5 weeks old and 6 cm tall. Plot the point (weeks = 5, height = 6).

pointErrors.feedback: You swapped them — weeks (5) is across, height (6) is up: plot (5, 6).
The height is 6, not 5 — go up to 6: plot (5, 6).
The plant is 5 weeks old — go across to 5: plot (5, 6).

widget.missFeedback: Across for weeks, up for height.
widget.successFeedback: Plotted — this older plant sits up and to the right of the younger one.

hints: The first number (weeks = 5) is the across-position.
The second number (height = 6) is the up-position.
Go across to 5, then up to 6: plot (5, 6).

steps.body: A scatter plot places one dot per item, pairing its two measurements as across and up.
takeaways: Each dot pairs two measurements: first across (x), then up (y).
One dot per item — keep the two numbers in order.
Scatter plots reveal relationships between two quantities.

concept.body: A scatter plot shows paired data with one dot per item. The first measurement is the across-position (x), the second is the up-position (y). Keep the two numbers in order.

explanationVariants: A dot at across-3, up-6 shows the pair (3, 6).
Read across (3) then up (6): the pair is (3, 6).

widget.prompt: A scatter-plot dot sits at across-position 3, up-position 6. What pair does it represent?

options.feedback: That swaps them — across (3) comes first: (3, 6).
A point is a PAIR, not a sum: (3, 6).
